definition: Soluble means able to dissolve in a liquid.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word soluble. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know soluble should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Washable-marker ink is soluble by design, which is why the art smock survives the school year.

Flour is mixable — beaten through water it makes a cloudy suspension, and by morning it has settled back out; soluble goes further than mixable: the solid truly disappears into the liquid and stays gone.
Instant goes past soluble — a plain soluble powder still wants a stir and a little patience; an instant one is engineered to vanish the moment it lands in the liquid.

Dissolvable says only that a thing can be dissolved — the plain, do-it-yourself word. Soluble is the term chemistry and labels prefer, the one that comes with conditions attached: soluble in what, at what temperature, how completely.

Dispersible means breaking into particles fine enough to spread evenly through a liquid without truly dissolving — the near-miss printed on medicine labels. Soluble goes the whole way: the solid passes into the liquid itself, invisibly, and stays gone.

Dissolve adds dis- (apart): to loosen a solid apart into a liquid, sugar into tea.

Rock candy begins with a fact children refuse to believe: sugar is so soluble that half a kilo will disappear into a single cup of near-boiling water.
The syrup looks like nothing.

Then a string goes in, the jar sits on a shelf, and for two weeks the trick runs backward — as the water cools and departs, the sugar has nowhere to stay, and it climbs out of hiding one glittering crystal at a time.
Soluble is the exact word for the sugar, because it means able to dissolve in a liquid — to break up into particles too small to see and vanish evenly into it.
The property belongs to the solid: sugar is soluble in water the way iron is not, and the whole candy trick is just that ability, lent and then taken back.

Soluble describes the solid that vanishes; this unit's solvent names the liquid that swallows it — keep the pair pointed in opposite directions, since a chemistry answer that swaps them is wrong twice.
Labels lean on soluble (water-soluble vitamins, soluble aspirin); in looser prose a soluble problem is one that can be solved, the same Latin loosening applied to a knot of a different kind.

The ocean is quietly drinking the sky.
Carbon dioxide is soluble in seawater, and the colder the water, the more of the gas it can take in.
Every year the surface ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of what human activity releases, the molecules passing invisibly into the water itself.
There is a cost: the added gas slowly turns seawater more acidic, which thins the shells of oysters, sea snails, and corals.
Scientists now track the ocean's chemistry the way doctors track blood pressure, reading in it the planet's changing breath.
